entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.3">Isa 18:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13040" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13041" type="x-p"/> The prophecy commences with <hi type="italic">hoi</hi>, which never signifies <hi type="italic">heus</hi>, but always <hi type="italic">vae</hi> (woe). Here, however, it differs from <reference osisRef="Isa.17.12">Isa 17:12</reference>, and is an expression of compassion (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Isa 55:1</reference>; Zec 2:10) rather than of anger; for the fact that the mighty Ethiopia is oppressed by the still mightier Asshur, is a humiliation which Jehovah has prepared for the former. <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1">Isa 18:1</reference>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Isa.18.2">Isa 18:2</reference></hi>: <hi type="italic">“Woe to the land of the whirring of wings, which is beyond the rivers of Cush, that sends ambassadors into the sea and in boats of papyrus over the face of the waters.”</hi> The land of Cush commences, according to <reference osisRef="Ezek.29.10">Eze 29:10</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.30.6">Isa 30:6</reference>), where Upper Egypt ends. The <hi type="italic">Sevēneh</hi> (<hi type="italic">Aswân</hi>), mentioned by Ezekiel, is the boundary-point at which the Nile enters <hi type="italic">Mizraim</hi> proper, and which is still a depot for goods coming from the south down the Nile. The <hi type="italic">naharē</hi>-<hi type="italic">Cush</hi> (rivers of Cush) are chiefly those that surround the Cushite <hi type="italic">Seba</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.10.7">Gen 10:7</reference>). This is the name given to the present Sennâr, the Meroitic island which is enclosed between the White and Blue Nile (the <hi type="italic">Astapos</hi> of Ptolemy, or the present <hi type="italic">Bahr</hi> <hi type="italic">el</hi>-<hi type="italic">Abyad</hi>, and the Astaboras of Ptolemy, or the present <hi type="italic">Bahr</hi> <hi type="italic">el</hi>-<hi type="italic">Azrak</hi>). According to the latest researches, more especially those of Speke, the White Nile, which takes its rise in the Lake of Nyanza, is the chief source of the Nile. The latter, and the Blue Nile, whose confluence (<hi type="italic">makran</hi>) with it takes place in lat. 15° 25´, are fed by many larger or smaller tributary streams (as well as mountain torrents); the Blue Nile even more than the Nile proper. And this abundance of water in the land to the south of <hi type="italic">Sevēnēh</hi>, and still farther south beyond <hi type="italic">Seba</hi> (or <hi type="italic">Meroë</hi>), might very well have been known to the prophet as a general fact. The land “beyond the rivers of Cush” is the land bounded by the sources of the Nile, i.e., (including Ethiopia itself in the stricter sense of the word) the south land under Ethiopian rule that lay still deeper in the heart of the country, the land of its African auxiliary tribes, whose names (which probably include the later Nubians and Abyssinians), as given in <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.3">2Ch 12:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Nah.3.9">Nah 3:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.30.5">Eze 30:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.46.9">Jer 46:9</reference>, suppose a minuteness of information which has not yet been attained by modern research. To this Ethiopia, which is designated by its farthest limits (compare Zep 3:10, where Wolff, in his book of Judith, erroneously supposes Media to be intended as the Asiatic Cush), the prophets give the strange name of <hi type="italic">eretz</hi> <hi type="italic">tziltzal</hi> <hi type="italic">cenâp</hi>. This has been interpreted as meaning “the land of the wings of an army with clashing arms” by Gesenius and others; but <hi type="italic">cenâphaim</hi> does not occur in this sense, like <hi type="italic">'agappim</hi> in Ezekiel. Others render it “the land of the noise of waves” (Umbreit); but <hi type="italic">cenâphaim</hi> cannot be used of waters except in such a connection as Isa 8:8. Moreover, <hi type="italic">tziltzal</hi> is not a fitting onomatopoetic word either for the clashing of arms or the noise of waves. Others, again, render it “the land of the double shadow” (Grotius, Vitringa, Knobel, and others); but, however appropriate this epithet might be to Ethiopia as a tropical land, it is very hazardous to take the word in a sense which is not sustained by the usage of the language; and the same objection may be brought against Luzzatto’s “land of the far-shadowing defence.” Shelling has also suggested another objection - namely, that the shadow thrown even in tropical lands is not a double one, falling northwards and southwards at the same time, and therefore that it cannot be figuratively described as double-winged. <hi type="italic">Tziltzal</hi> <hi type="italic">cenâphaim</hi> is the buzzing of the wings of insects, with which Egypt and Ethiopia swarmed on account of the climate and the abundance of water: צלצל, <hi type="italic">constr</hi>. צלצל, <hi type="italic">tinnitus</hi>, <hi type="italic">stridor</hi>, a primary meaning from which the other three meanings of the word-cymbal, harpoon (a whirring dart), and grasshopper<note placement="foot">Schröring supposes <hi type="italic">tziltzal</hi> to be the <hi type="italic">scarabaeus sacer</hi> (Linn.); but it would be much more natural, if any particular animal is intended, to think of the <hi type="italic">tzaltzalya</hi>, as it is called in the language of the Gallas, the <hi type="italic">tzetze</hi> in the Betschuana language, the most dreaded diptera of the interior of Africa, a species of <hi type="italic">glossina</hi> which attacks all the larger <hi type="italic">mammalia</hi> (though not men). Vid., Hartmann, <hi type="italic">Naturgeschichtlich-medic</hi>. <hi type="italic">Skizze der Nilländer</hi>, Abth. i. p. 205.</note>  - are derived. In <reference osisRef="Isa.7.18">Isa 7:18</reference> the forces of Egypt are called “the fly from the end of the rivers of Egypt.” Here Egypt and Ethiopia are called the land of the whirring of wings, inasmuch as the prophet had in his mind, under the designation of swarms of insects, the motley swarms of different people included in this great kingdom that were so fabulously strange to an Asiatic. Within this great kingdom messengers were now passing to and fro upon its great waters in boats of papyrus (on <hi type="italic">gōme</hi>, Copt. <hi type="italic">‛gōme</hi>, Talm. <hi type="italic">gâmi</hi>, see at <reference osisRef="Job.8.11">Job 8:11</reference>), Greek βαρίδες παπύριναι (βαρίς, from the Egyptian <hi type="italic">bari</hi>, <hi type="italic">bali</hi>, a barque). In such vessels as these, and with Egyptian tackle, they went as far as the remote island of Taprobane. The boats were made to clap together (<hi type="italic">pilcatiles</hi>), so as to be carried past the cataracts (Parthey on <hi type="italic">Plutarch. de Iside</hi>, pp. 198-9). And it is to these messengers in their paper boats that the appeal of the prophet is addressed. <div eID="gen13041" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13042" type="x-p"/> He sends them home; and what they are to say to their own people is generalized into an announcement to the whole earth. <hi type="italic">“Go, swift messengers, to the people stretched out and polished, to the terrible people far away on the other side, to the nation of command upon command and treading down, whose land rivers cut through. All ye possessors of the globe and inhabitants of the earth, when a banner rises on the mountains, look ye; and when they blow the trumpets, hearken!”</hi> We learn from what follows to what it is that the attention of Ethiopia and all the nations of the earth is directed: it is the destruction of Asshur by Jehovah. They are to attend, when they observe the two signals, the banner and the trumpet-blast; these are decisive moments. Because Jehovah was about to deliver the world from the conquering might of Assyria, against which the Ethiopian kingdom was now summoning all the means of self-defence, the prophet sends the messengers home. Their own people, to which he sends them home, are elaborately described. They are <hi type="italic">memusshâk</hi>, stretched out, i.e., very tall (lxx ἔθνος μετέωρον), just as the Sabaeans are said to have been in Isa 45:14. They are also <hi type="italic">mōrât</hi> = <hi type="italic">memorât</hi> (Ges. §52, Anm. 6), smoothed, <hi type="italic">politus</hi>, i.e., either not disfigured by an ugly growth of hair, or else, without any reference to depilation, but rather with reference to the bronze colour of their skin, smooth and shining with healthy freshness. The description which Herodotus gives of the Ethiopians, μέγιστοι καὶ κάλλιστοι ἀνθρώπων πάντων (iii. 20), quite answers to these first two predicates. They are still further described, with reference to the wide extent of their kingdom, which reached to the remotest south, as “the terrible nation והלאה מן־הוּא,” i.e., from this point, where the prophet meets with the messengers, farther and farther off (compare <reference osisRef="1Sam.20.21-1Sam.20.22">1Sa 20:21-22</reference>, but not <reference osisRef="1Sam.18.9">1Sa 18:9</reference>, where the expression has a chronological meaning, which would be less suitable here, where everything is so pictorial, and which is also to be rejected, because מן־הוּא cannot be equivalent to הוּא מאשׁר; cf., <reference osisRef="Nah.2.9">Nah 2:9</reference>). We may see from <reference osisRef="Isa.28.10">Isa 28:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.13">Isa 28:13</reference>, what <hi type="italic">kâv</hi> (<hi type="italic">kăv</hi>, with connecting accusatives and before <hi type="italic">makkeph</hi>), a measuring or levelling line, signifies, when used by the prophet with the reduplication which he employs here: it is a people of “command upon command,” - that is to say, a commanding nation; (according to Ewald, Knobel, and others, <hi type="italic">kâv</hi> is equivalent to the Arabic <hi type="italic">kūwe</hi>, strength, a nation of double or gigantic strength.) “<hi type="italic">A people of treading down</hi>” (sc., of others; <hi type="italic">mebūsah</hi> is a second genitive to <hi type="italic">goi</hi>), i.e., one which subdues and tramples down wherever it appears. These are all distinctive predicates - a nation of imposing grandeur, a ruling and conquering nation. The last predicate extols its fertile land. בּזא we take not in the sense of diripere, or as equivalent to <hi type="italic">bâzaz</hi>, like מאס, to melt, equivalent to <hi type="italic">mâsas</hi>, but in the sense of <hi type="italic">findere</hi>, i.e., as equivalent to בזע, like גּמא, to sip = גּמע. For it is no praise to say that a land is scoured out, or washed away, by rivers. Böttcher, who is wrong in describing this chapter as “perhaps the most difficult in the whole of the Old Testament,” very aptly compares with it the expression used by Herodotus (ii. 108), κατετμήθη ἡ Αἴγυπτος. But why this strange elaboration instead of the simple name? There is a divine irony in the fact that a nation so great and glorious, and (though not without reason, considering its natural gifts) so full of self-consciousness, should be thrown into such violent agitation in the prospect of the danger that threatened it, and should be making such strenuous exertions to avert that danger, when Jehovah the God of Israel was about to destroy the threatening power itself in a night, and consequently all the care and trouble of Ethiopia were utterly needless.

The last predicate extols its fertile land. בּזא we take not in the sense of diripere, or as equivalent to bâzaz , like מאס, to melt, equivalent to mâsas , but in the sense of findere , i.e., as equivalent to בזע, like גּמא, to sip = גּמע. For it is no praise to say that a land is scoured out, or washed away, by rivers. Böttcher, who is wrong in describing this chapter as “perhaps the most difficult in the whole of the Old Testament,” very aptly compares with it the expression used by Herodotus (ii. 108), κατετμήθη ἡ Αἴγυπτος. But why this strange elaboration instead of the simple name? There is a divine irony in the fact that a nation so great and glorious, and (though not without reason, considering its natural gifts) so full of self-consciousness, should be thrown into such violent agitation in the prospect of the danger that threatened it, and should be making such strenuous exertions to avert that danger, when Jehovah the God of Israel was about to destroy the threatening power itself in a night, and consequently all the care and trouble of Ethiopia were utterly needless.

entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.18.4-Isa.18.6">Isa 18:4-6</reference> <div eID="gen13042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13043" type="x-p"/> The prophet knows for certain that the messengers may be home and announce this act of Jehovah to their own people and to all the world. <hi type="italic">“For thus hath Jehovah spoken to me: I will be still, and will observe upon my throne during clear weather in sunshine, during a cloud of dew in the heat of harvest. For before the harvest, when the blossom falls off, and the fruit becomes the ripening grape: then will He cut off the branches with pruning-hooks; and the tendrils He removes, breaks off. They are left altogether to the birds of prey on the mountains, and to the cattle of the land; and the birds of prey summer thereon, and all the cattle of the land will winter thereon.”</hi> The prophecy explains itself here, as is very frequently the case, especially with Isaiah; for the literal words of v. 6 show us unquestionably what it is that Jehovah will allow to develop itself so prosperously under favourable circumstances, and without any interposition on His part, until He suddenly and violently puts an end to the whole, must as it is approaching perfect maturity. It is the might of Assyria. Jehovah quietly looks on from the heavenly seat of His glorious presence, without disturbing the course of the thing intended. This quietness, however, is not negligence, but, as the hortative expressions show, a well-considered resolution. The two <hi type="italic">Caphs</hi> in v. 4 are not comparative, but indicate the time. He remains quiet whilst there is clear weather with sunshine (עלי indicating continuance, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.8.18">Jer 8:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.32">1Sa 14:32</reference>), and whilst there is a dew-cloud in the midst of that warmth, which is so favourable for the harvest, by causing the plants that have been thoroughly heated in the day and refreshed at night by the dew, to shoot up and ripen with rapidity and luxuriance. The plant thought of, as v. 5 clearly shows, is the vine. By <hi type="italic">liphnē</hi> <hi type="italic">kâtzir</hi> (before the harvest) we are either to understand the period just before the wheat-harvest, which coincides with the flowering of the grape; or, since Isaiah uses <hi type="italic">kâtzir</hi> for <hi type="italic">bâzri</hi> in <reference osisRef="Isa.16.9">Isa 16:9</reference>, the time at the close of the summer, immediately preceding the vintage. Here again the <hi type="italic">Caph</hi> indicates the time. When the blossoming is over, so that the flower fades away, and the fruit that has set becomes a ripening grape (<hi type="italic">boser</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Job.15.33">Job 15:33</reference>, not in the sense of <hi type="italic">labruscum</hi>, but of <hi type="italic">omphax</hi>; and <hi type="italic">gâmal</hi>, <hi type="italic">maturescere</hi>, as in Num 17:8, <hi type="italic">maturare</hi>), He cuts off the branches (<hi type="italic">zalzalilm</hi>, from <hi type="italic">zilzēl</hi>, to swing to and fro; compare the Arabic <hi type="italic">dâliye</hi>, a vine-branch, from <hi type="italic">dalâ</hi>, to hang long and loose) upon which the nearly ripened grapes are hanging, and removes or nips off<note placement="foot">התז = התז with a pausal sharpening of the <hi type="italic">tzere</hi>, which is lengthened by the tone, from <hi type="italic">tâzaz</hi> or <hi type="italic">tı̄z</hi> in post-biblical Hebrew, to knock off, knock to pieces, or weaken (compare <hi type="italic">tâshash</hi>). On this change of vowels in pause, see at <reference osisRef="Gen.17.14">Gen 17:14</reference>; and compare Olshausen, §91, d. For an example of the post-biblical use of the word, vid., <hi type="italic">b. Sanhedrin</hi> 102 <hi type="italic">a</hi>, “like two sticks <hi type="italic">hammattı̄zōth</hi>,” i.e., one of which “hits the other in two” (<hi type="italic">hittiz</hi>, apparently from <hi type="italic">tūz</hi>, or <hi type="italic">tiz</hi>, like <hi type="italic">hinnı̄ach</hi> from <hi type="italic">nuach</hi>).</note> the tendrils (<hi type="italic">netishoth</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.5.10">Jer 5:10</reference>, from <hi type="italic">nâtash</hi>, to stretch far out; <hi type="italic">niphal</hi>, to twist about a long way, <reference osisRef="Isa.16.8">Isa 16:8</reference>, compare <reference osisRef="Jer.48.32">Jer 48:32</reference>); an intentional asyndeton with a pictorial sound. The words of Jehovah concerning Himself have here passed imperceptibly into words of the prophet concerning Jehovah. The ripening grapes, as <reference osisRef="Isa.18.6">Isa 18:6</reference> now explains, are the Assyrians, who were not far from the summit of their power; the fruit-branches that are cut off and nipped in pieces are their corpses, which are now through both summer and winter the food of swarms of summer birds, as well as of beasts of prey that remain the whole winter through. entries.content_osis: <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference> <div eID="gen13043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13044" type="x-p"/> What effect this act of Jehovah would have upon the Ethiopian kingdom, if it should now take place, is described in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.7">Isa 18:7</reference> : <hi type="italic">“At that time will there be offered as a homage to Jehovah of hosts a nation stretched out and polished, and from a terrible people, far away on the other side; a nation of command upon command and treading down, whose land rivers cut through, at the place of the name of Jehovah of hosts, the mountain of Zion.”</hi> עם (a people), at the commencement, cannot possibly be equivalent to מעם (from a people). If it were taken in this sense, it would be necessary to make the correction accordingly, as Knobel has done; but the important parallels in <reference osisRef="Isa.66.20">Isa 66:20</reference> and Zep 3:10 are against this. Consequently <hi type="italic">‛am</hi> and <hi type="italic">goi</hi> (people and nation) must be rendered as subjects; and the מן in מעם must be taken as partitive. Ethiopia is offered, i.e., offers itself, as a free-will offering to Jehovah, impelled irresistibly by the force of the impression made by the mighty act of Jehovah, or, as it is expressed in “the Titan among the Psalms” (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.32">Psa 68:32</reference>, probably a Davidic psalm of the time of Hezekiah), “there come kingdoms of splendour out of Egypt; Cush rapidly stretches out its hands to <hi type="italic">Elohim</hi>.” In order that the greatness of this spiritual conquest might be fully appreciated, the description of this strangely glorious people is repeated here; and with this poetical rounding, the prophecy itself, which was placed as a kind of overture before the following <hi type="italic">massa Mitzraim</hi> when the prophet collected the whole of his prophecies together, is brought to a close. The Oracle Concerning Egypt  - Isaiah 19 <div eID="gen13044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13045" type="x-p"/> The three prophecies in <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.7.19">Isa 18:1-7, 19</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference> really form a trilogy. The first (<reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference>), which, like chapter 1, the introduction to the whole, is without any special heading, treats in language of the sublimest pathos of <hi type="italic">Ethiopia</hi>. The second (chapter 19) treats in a calmer and more descriptive tone of <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi>. The third (<reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference>) treats of both <hi type="italic">Egypt</hi> and <hi type="italic">Ethiopia</hi> in the style of historic prose. The kingdom to which all three prophecies refer is one and the same, viz., the Egypto-Ethiopian kingdom; but whilst <reference osisRef="Isa.18.1-Isa.18.7">Isa 18:1-7</reference> refers to the ruling nation, chapter 19 treats of the conquered one, and <reference osisRef="Isa.20.1-Isa.20.6">Isa 20:1-6</reference> embraces both together. The reason why such particular attention is given to Egypt in the prophecy, is that no nation on earth was so mixed up with the history of the kingdom of God, from the patriarchal times downwards, as Egypt was. And because Israel, as the law plainly enjoined upon it, was never to forget that it had been sheltered for a long time in Egypt, and there had grown into a great nation, and had received many benefits; whenever prophecy has to speak concerning Egypt, it is quite as earnest in its promises as it is in its threats. And thus the <hi type="italic">massa</hi> of Isaiah falls into two distinct halves, viz., a threatening one (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.15">Isa 19:1-15</reference>), and a promising one (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.18-Isa.19.25">Isa 19:18-25</reference>); whilst between the judgment and the salvation (in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.16">Isa 19:16</reference> and <reference osisRef="Isa.19.17">Isa 19:17</reference>) there stands the alarm, forming as it were a connecting bridge between the two. And just in proportion as the coil of punishments is unfolded on the one hand by the prophet, the promise is also unfolded in just as many stages on the other; and moving on in ever new grooves, rises at length to such a height, that it breaks not only through the limits of contemporaneous history, but even through those of the Old Testament itself, and speaks in the spiritual language of the world-embracing love of the New Testament.  <chapter eID="Isa.18"/> <div eID="gen13045" type="x-p"/>
